For he had a vow. Probably the vow of a Nazirite (

).  It was taken in gratitude for deliverance from sickness or other misfortune.  The hair of the head was shaved and then allowed to grow, and after a certain period the person went to Jerusalem and made an offering of the hair, which had grown, in the interval.  Then the head was again shaved.

segments: Gallio was proconsul. Gallio was a brother of the philosopher Seneca, Nero's tutor, and an uncle of the poet Lucan.  He had been consul at Rome, and was afterward sent out to rule in Achaia.  The title 'proconsul' proves that Achaia was a province belonging to the Roman senate, not to the emperor.  See note on

entries.title: Acts 18:14
segments: Gallio said, etc.  He determined to have nothing to do with the complaint of the Jews, even before Paul was heard.  He was contemptuously indifferent to Jewish laws and customs.

entries.title: Acts 18:17
segments:
Sosthenes. The crowd thought that a Jew could be safely beaten after the Roman proconsul had decided that a Jewish wrangle was not worth bothering about.
 

 
For none of these things. That is, neither for the unjust assault upon Sosthenes and the complaint against Paul, nor the general question of Jewish religious rights and privileges.

entries.title: Acts 18:19
segments: Ephesus. The capital city of the Roman province of Asia.  It was celebrated for its temple of Diana and for its theater, which seated 24,500.  In Paul's time its population of 225,000 made it next to Alexandria in size among the cities of the East.  From about 300 AD it became a great center of Christian pilgrimage because of its association with Paul, Timothy, and the apostle John who died there in 100 AD.

entries.title: Acts 18:23
segments: Galatia, and Phrygia. See notes on

.  Starting again from Antioch in Syria, he revisited the churches founded in the cities of his first journey, namely, Derbe, Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch in Pisidia; thence he proceeded to the churches in the northerly cities of Galatia.  Returning he crossed through Phrygia and Lydia to Ephesus, where he remained two years.  From Ephesus he sailed north to the coast of Macedonia, revisiting the churches and going south by land through Greece as far as Corinth.  Hearing of a plot against him by the Jews, he determined to return home by way of Macedonia, sailing from Philippi to Troas, Assos, Mytelene, Chios, Samos, Miletus, Cos, Rhodes, and Patara; thence direct to Tyre on the Phoenician coast.  From Tyre he went to Ptolemais and Caesarea, and thence to Jerusalem.

entries.title: Acts 18:26
segments: Expounded unto him, etc.  An important and timely help, greatly strengthening the usefulness of Apollos.  He knew Jesus as the Messiah, as the Savior of the world from sin; but how much more he must have learned from his two friends, who had been instructed by Paul!
